description: I’m Egli, a CS student passionate about game making. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are tackling the Space Mission Design Game, aiming to turn real NASA mission data and orbital engineering constraints into a fun experience. Let’s team up and build something.
summary: MARGIN puts you in charge of a robotic science mission from proposal to final data. Pick a science goal, build a spacecraft part by part, choose a rocket and trajectory, defend the design at a Review Board, fly a time-compressed mission full of real NASA history, and finish with a debrief that replays your mission with one decision changed at a time to show which choices mattered.
details:
MARGIN is a browser game where you lead a robotic science mission from proposal to final data. You pick a science goal (Mars, Jupiter or the Moon), each with a cost cap. Then you build a spacecraft part by part: instruments, power, antenna, shielding, propulsion and orbit. Next you choose a rocket and trajectory, defend the design at a Review Board, and fly a time-compressed mission where real problems from NASA history become decisions you have to make. It ends with a debrief that replays your mission with one decision changed at a time, using the same random seed, so you can see which choices actually mattered.

Underneath is a TypeScript simulator that links the trade-offs together the way they’re linked in real mission design:

  • Launch capacity is checked against launch energy (C3).
  • Propellant mass comes from the rocket equation, so extra mass needs more propellant, which adds more mass.
  • Solar power falls off with the square of distance from the Sun, and batteries have to last through eclipses.
  • The radio link is modelled on the Deep Space Network.
  • Orbit insertion and radiation dose are checked against electronics tolerance.

Here’s an example. NASA Ames trajectory data gives a direct route to Jupiter a C3 of 77.5 km²/s² and an Earth gravity-assist route 26.5 km²/s². With NASA Launch Services Program curves, that’s the difference between about 978 kg and 5,158 kg of capacity on the same rocket. The cost is 576 more days in cruise.

Benefits

  • Students make the same coupled decisions an engineering team makes, and the lessons come from physics rather than arbitrary game rules.
  • Every number links to its NASA source. Each data record is flagged as verified, approximate or tuned for gameplay, so players and teachers can tell real figures from game assumptions.
  • A failed or partly successful mission still teaches something. The debrief shows the top decisions that drove the outcome, and a Monte Carlo estimate shows how often your design succeeds across 50 simulated runs.
  • It’s free and runs in any modern browser, with no install, no account and no runtime API calls.

Intended impact

We want students and space fans to understand why real missions look the way they do: why Juno flew a longer route, why it carried a titanium radiation vault, and why “margin” is the difference between surviving a surprise and losing the mission. MARGIN is built for classrooms. We drafted discussion prompts (“Why would a team accept a longer trip?” and “Which design change helped, and what did it cost?”) and a simple pilot plan. We haven’t run a pilot yet, so we report no participant results.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand (state), Zod (data validation), Motion (animation) and Vitest (tests).
  • Hosting: GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.
  • Fonts: Space Grotesk and JetBrains Mono (SIL Open Font License).
  • Hardware: no special hardware; it runs on any device with a modern browser.
  • NASA data: JPL planetary elements and Horizons, NSSDCA fact sheets, NASA Ames Trajectory Browser, NASA Launch Services Program performance curves, the DSN Link Design Handbook, the Small Spacecraft State-of-the-Art report, the CCMC DONKI space-weather archive, the Lessons Learned database, and mission press kits and reports.
  • AI assistance (disclosed): Claude Code and OpenAI Codex helped with code, tests, documentation and drafting approximate seed data. Approximate values stay flagged in the catalog.

What makes it creative

  1. Hindsight: the debrief re-runs your exact mission, same seed and same events, with one choice changed at a time. This shows cause and effect instead of just giving a score.
  2. Real NASA history as gameplay: 14 decision cards are based on real events, such as Juno’s engine valve problem and Lunar Trailblazer’s loss of contact. Solar storms are replayed from NASA’s DONKI archive.
  3. You vs. History: your spacecraft is shown side by side with the real mission that tackled the same science (Juno, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter or Lunar Prospector).

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific validity: automated tests check a modelled Juno orbit insertion against the historical burn and compare planet positions with JPL Horizons.
  • Honesty about data: we never invent historical facts. Values tuned for gameplay are labelled as such in the game and in the code.
  • Accessibility and reach: no login, no install, deterministic replays so teachers and judges can reproduce results, and a guided Jupiter demo.
  • NASA branding rules: no NASA logos, insignia, mission patches or flags. We only use credited NASA imagery and no AI-generated images, video or audio.
  • Scope: we had a 36-hour build across three tracks (engine, data and interface), with fixed scope tiers so the core experience shipped first.
